prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

upon how un/safe people felt in different spaces. People referred to a range of issues in the built environment that contributed to feelings of discomfort and anxiety: this included road crossings that were difficult to navigate, a lack of audible signals, poor street lighting, and street furniture and parked SOCIAL & CULTURAL GEOGRAPHY 169 cars that presented obstacles. Robert (VI), for example, explained his anxiety around road crossings: It’s making sure all the audible signals work to let me know when it’s safe to cross. Like there’s a lot around the city that don’t work, so before I get there I’m like God, I hope there’s someone around that I can ask to cross because it makes me feel really nervous. Participants who were Deaf or hard of hearing described the fear of being taken by surprise by cars coming up behind them in street spaces, while some people who used wheelchairs described feeling unsafe as they had to travel on the road due to inaccessible pavements. Marian (MI), who lived in a small flat in a busy inner city area marked by socio- economic deprivation, described how inaccessibility led to her experiencing verbal abuse when out in her wheelchair: ‘Like when I’m on the road, yeah, I’d get beeps – “You f***ing – ” you know what I mean? – “You dope” – there’s a lot of places where I can’t get up on paths’. People with VI also described feelings of insecurity that could result from disorientating aspects of the physical environment. Highlighting the significance of walls as physical markers to assist with navigation, for example, many people discussed the difficulties of navigating large shopping centres and open spaces. As Deirdre who lives alone in a city centre and uses a guide dog, said, ‘I steer clear of plazas because to me they are just massive areas with no sense of knowing where I am’. While some participants described avoiding large shopping centres, for others they were a space of comfort and security. Aoife described her local shopping centre as a safe space because it is was enclosed and easy to navigate in her wheelchair. She articulated access not just in terms of physical environment – the ability of a café or restaurant to accommodate her wheelchair, for example, – but also by affectual encounters of welcome by staff. Robert similarly described this experience of welcome, stating, ‘There’s a bar we go to and they know a few of us in there. So they say ‘Oh your particular spot is not free . . . we’ll bring you down to the end of the bar where there’s a seat’. Particpants’ narratives demonstrate the interconnections that exist between the mate- riality of environments, objects and bodies, to create moments of comfort, but also of anxiety for disabled people as they navigate everyday spaces. These interconnections become particularly visible in the following account from Martin of navigating the streetscape near his home with his white cane. Recounting the incident as we walked, he stated: I was just about to cross the road

it is higher than on arterial or residential streets, but in order to offer cycling infrastructure that can be used relaxed and stress-free, planners should decide for physically separated cycle paths if possible. The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow. The shared space is evaluated negatively on the Interaction cluster. Road users are forced to interact

As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

People referred to a range of issues in the built environment that contributed to feelings of discomfort and anxiety: this included road crossings that were difficult to navigate, a lack of audible signals, poor street lighting, and street furniture and parked SOCIAL & CULTURAL GEOGRAPHY 169 cars that presented obstacles. Robert (VI), for example, explained his anxiety around road crossings: It’s making sure all the audible signals work to let me know when it’s safe to cross. Like there’s a lot around the city that don’t work, so before I get there I’m like God, I hope there’s someone around that I can ask to cross because it makes me feel really nervous. Participants who were Deaf or hard of hearing described the fear of being taken by surprise by cars coming up behind them in street spaces, while some people who used wheelchairs described feeling unsafe as they had to travel on the road due to inaccessible pavements. Marian (MI), who lived in a small flat in a busy inner city area marked by socio- economic deprivation, described how inaccessibility led to her experiencing verbal abuse when out in her wheelchair: ‘Like when I’m on the road, yeah, I’d get beeps – “You f***ing – ” you know what I mean? – “You dope” – there’s a lot of places where I can’t get up on paths’. People with VI also described feelings of insecurity that could result from disorientating aspects of the physical environment. Highlighting the significance of walls as physical markers to assist with navigation, for example, many people discussed the difficulties of navigating large shopping centres and open spaces. As Deirdre who lives alone in a city centre and uses a guide dog, said, ‘I steer clear of plazas because to me they are just massive areas with no sense of knowing where I am’. While some participants described avoiding large shopping centres, for others they were a space of comfort and security. Aoife described her local shopping centre as a safe space because it is was enclosed and easy to navigate in her wheelchair. She articulated access not just in terms of physical environment – the ability of a café or restaurant to accommodate her wheelchair, for example, – but also by affectual encounters of welcome by staff. Robert similarly described this experience of welcome, stating, ‘There’s a bar we go to and they know a few of us in there. So they say ‘Oh your particular spot is not free . . . we’ll bring you down to the end of the bar where there’s a seat’. Particpants’ narratives demonstrate the interconnections that exist between the mate- riality of environments, objects and bodies, to create moments of comfort, but also of anxiety for disabled people as they navigate everyday spaces. These interconnections become particularly visible in the following account from Martin of navigating the streetscape near his home with his white cane. The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow.
